subject: Chemistry
title: Emulsifiers: Making the Unmixable Mix
description: A quick win: understand Emulsifiers: Making the Unmixable Mix.

hook.text: Mayonnaise is 80% oil and 20% water—yet it's a smooth, creamy sauce. Egg yolk makes this possible.

buildup.text: Egg yolk contains lecithin—a phospholipid with a water-loving head and a fat-loving tail.

discovery.text: Lecithin molecules sit at the oil-water interface, stabilizing tiny oil droplets in a water-based emulsion.

twist.text: Without the emulsifier, mayonnaise separates in minutes. With it, it stays stable for months.

climax.text: Processed foods use emulsifiers like soy lecithin and polysorbate 80. They're in ice cream, bread, and chocolate.

punchline.text: One molecule bridges oil and water. That's why mayonnaise exists.

quiz.question: How does egg yolk make mayonnaise possible?
options: Lecithin in the yolk stabilizes oil droplets in a water-based emulsion
The protein in yolk hardens into a solid framework
The cholesterol in yolk dissolves the oil completely

details.summary: Emulsifiers are molecules with both hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends that stabilize mixtures of oil and water that would otherwise separate. Lecithin in egg yolks coats fat droplets with a charged surface, keeping them dispersed in the water phase of mayonnaise and other emulsified sauces.
details.whyItMatters: Emulsification underpins food science, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical formulation. Without emulsifiers, products from salad dressing to vaccines and lotions would separate into unusable layers.
takeaways: Emulsifiers have water-loving and oil-loving ends on the same molecule
Lecithin from egg yolks is nature's most versatile food emulsifier
Emulsion stability depends on droplet size and surfactant packing

faq.question: Why does mayonnaise stay mixed instead of separating like oil and vinegar?
faq.answer: Lecithin and proteins in egg yolks coat each tiny oil droplet with a charged membrane that repels other droplets. Vigorous whisking breaks oil into droplets small enough for the emulsifier to fully coat. The electrical repulsion between coated droplets prevents them from merging.

faq.question: What causes an emulsion to break or separate?
faq.answer: Emulsions break when the stabilizing layer around droplets is disrupted by temperature changes, excessive shaking, acid addition, or insufficient emulsifier. Droplets then merge through coalescence, and gravity separates the lighter oil phase from the denser water phase.
